State and metro employment: Third quarter 2026Posted on November 23, 2026

SHARE THIS PAGE:

Link Copied

National employment growth in the third quarter of 2026 accelerated slightly to 0.4% compared to one year ago. However, state-level results display wider variation, with 10 states losing jobs while the remaining 40 grew strongly compared to one year ago. The median state also experienced job growth of roughly 0.4%. Moreover, growth accelerated in 37 states between the second and third quarter.

The FRED map above shows the percent change from a year ago in employment in each state during the third quarter. South Carolina and Utah exhibited the strongest growth, with net job gains of 2.3% and 1.4%, respectively. The District of Columbia and Montana saw the largest net job loss at 3.6% and 0.8%, respectively.

At the metro level, job growth on average displayed slightly weaker trends than the state level data, with the median MSA experiencing slight job gain of 0.3% in the third quarter of 2026 relative to one year ago. The Bloomington, Indiana, MSA had the largest net job loss at 3.4%. In contrast, the Sandusky, Ohio, MSA exhibited the strongest job growth at 4.4%. These numbers tend to vary greatly from quarter to quarter, with even greater sampling errors than the errors at the state and national levels. So, be careful not to read too much into these data.

How these maps were created: Search FRED for “total nonfarm employees in Missouri” (or any other state). Click “View Map” and then “Edit Map.” Change the units to “Percent Change from Year Ago” and the frequency to quarterly with aggregation method “End of Period.” Under “Format,” select “User Defined Method” for how to group the data: Switch the number of color groups to 3 and change the colors to red for states that shed jobs (or a value less than or equal to 0), light yellow for states with modest job growth (or less than 0.7), and dark green for states with strong growth (or a value large enough to incorporate the rest of the states). For the second map, repeat the process with an MSA—St. Louis, for example.

Suggested by Charles Gascon and Rehann Silvanus.
